tldr: Voyager is a GPT-4 Minecraft agent that learns open-endedly with no gradients: an automatic curriculum proposes tasks, a library of self-verified executable code skills supplies reusable behavior, and environment feedback, execution errors and self-verification refine the code — 3.3× more items than baselines.
method: Three GPT-4 modules over a MineDojo + Mineflayer bot (§2). (1) Automatic curriculum: GPT-4 (temperature 0.1) gets the directive 'discover as many diverse things as possible', the agent state (inventory, equipment, biome, time, health/hunger, position, nearby blocks/entities), completed and failed task lists, and GPT-3.5 self-asked Q&A context, then emits the next task. (2) Skill library: each solved task is committed as a JavaScript program calling hand-written control primitives, keyed by the embedding of a GPT-3.5-written description; for a new task the plan plus environment feedback retrieve the top-5 skills into the code prompt. (3) Iterative prompting: execute the generated program, feed back bot.chat() progress messages and interpreter error traces, re-prompt GPT-4 to refine, and repeat; a separate GPT-4 self-verification agent returns success plus a critique. Success commits the skill and queries the curriculum again; four failed code rounds trigger a new task. No fine-tuning, no parameter access.
results: Exploration (Fig. 1): Voyager discovers 63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations, 3.3× more than ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT, which barely progress against the abstract goal.

Tech tree (Table 1, prompting iterations to unlock, 3 trials): Voyager 6±2 wooden, 11±2 stone, 21±7 iron (3/3 each) and, uniquely, diamond at 102 (1/3); AutoGPT 92±72 / 94±72 / 135±103 (3/3) but never diamond; Voyager without the skill library 7±2 / 9±4 / 29±11 but never diamond; ReAct and Reflexion never unlock even wooden (0/3). That is 15.3×, 8.5× and 6.4× faster than the best baseline at the three levels.
Map coverage (Fig. 7): Voyager travels 2.3× longer distances across diverse terrain, while baselines stay confined to local areas.

Zero-shot generalization (Table 2, fresh world, cleared inventory, 50-iteration cap): Voyager solves all four unseen tasks at 19±3 (Diamond Pickaxe), 18±7 (Golden Sword), 21±5 (Lava Bucket) and 18±2 (Compass) iterations, 3/3 each; no baseline solves any (0/3), and AutoGPT given Voyager's skill library reaches only 39 (1/3), 30 (1/3), 0/3 and 30 (2/3).

Ablations (Fig. 9): a random curriculum costs 93% of discovered items, deleting self-verification costs 73%, removing the skill library plateaus later stages, and swapping GPT-4 for GPT-3.5 in code generation yields 5.7× fewer unique items. Skill retrieval scores 80.2±3.0 top-1 and 96.5±0.3 top-5 accuracy over 309 samples (Table A.4).
advantages: Skills are executable, interpretable, compositional code, not text memories: each one is admitted only after environment execution and critic-confirmed success, is built on named control primitives, and composes into harder programs — the mechanism that lets later skills stand on earlier ones and keeps the agent off the plateau seen when the library is ablated.

The library transfers as an artifact: it works in a newly instantiated world and is plug-and-play for another agent, lifting AutoGPT from 0/3 on every unseen task to partial success on three of four — the paper's clearest evidence that the learned skills, not the prompting style, carry the capability.

Component attribution is measured rather than asserted: curriculum (−93%), self-verification (−73%), skill library and GPT-4-class code generation (5.7× items) are each individually ablated, isolating what actually drives open-ended progress.

Whole loop is gradient-free on a blackbox GPT-4: the model is queried through prompting only, needs no trajectory data, reward model or fine-tuning, and the results are robust across gpt-4-0314 and gpt-4-0613.
limitations: Cost and model lock-in: GPT-4 is 15× more expensive than GPT-3.5, yet the paper states the loop requires GPT-4's code-generation quality (GPT-3.5 loses 5.7× in unique items) and that open-source LLMs cannot substitute at the time of writing.

Failure modes persist despite the loop: the agent still gets stuck on some skills, self-verification misses cases (it does not read spider string as evidence of killing a spider), the curriculum hallucinates non-existent items such as 'copper sword' and 'copper chestplate', and generated code misuses invalid fuel (cobblestone) or calls absent API functions.

No perception: the GPT-4 API is text-only, so Voyager sees inventory/state text rather than pixels and acts through the high-level Mineflayer API — the paper explicitly declines comparison with pixel-and-low-level-control agents and leaves vision to future multimodal models.

The hardest demonstrations are human-scaffolded: building a Nether Portal or a house required a human as critic and as curriculum, and the domain is Minecraft only; transferring to physical robots would need added safety constraints.
fits: Stage 4's founding skill-library result and the ancestor of code-skill substrates (AgentFactory, DGM-lineage). Read next to Reflexion (2303.11366) — verbal reflections vs verified executable skills — and ExpeL/A-MEM for memory without environment-verified code. Pairs with the runnable Voyager repo card (stage 10) and MineDojo/Mineflayer as the substrate.
reading: §2.1–2.3 for the three modules (curriculum prompt, skill-library key/value + top-5 retrieval, the four-round iterative-prompting loop), §3.3 with Tables 1–2 for the numbers, §4 limits, B.4.4 for 96.5% retrieval accuracy.

Two cautions: Table 1's stream extraction is column-scrambled, so the rows cited come from the -layout rendering (AutoGPT 92/94/135; Voyager 6/11/21, diamond 102 (1/3)); and the 15.3×/8.5×/6.4× figures are the paper's own ratios, which recompute correctly from those rows (92/6, 94/11, 135/21). High confidence. The floor card's claims (3.3× items, faster tech tree, compounding skill library, hallucination/frozen-model limits) all hold; it omitted the verification-gated admission mechanism, baseline denominators, zero-shot table and ablation magnitudes, which this card adds.
